title: Polar Form
body:
**Polar form** writes a complex number by *where it points and how far out it is*, rather than
by its real and imaginary parts. For $z = a + bi$ plotted at $(a,b)$ in the complex plane:

$$
z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)
$$

- $r = |z| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ is the **modulus**, the distance from the origin
- $\theta = \arg z$ is the **argument**, the angle from the positive real axis

with $a = r\cos\theta$ and $b = r\sin\theta$ going back the other way. The same polar-versus-
rectangular choice as in [[Multiple Integration]], applied to $\mathbb{C}$.

Recovering $\theta$ from $a$ and $b$: $\tan\theta = b/a$, **but check the quadrant**.
$\arctan$ returns values in $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$ only, so it cannot tell $1+i$ from $-1-i$. This is
the same reason programming languages provide `atan2(b, a)` with two arguments rather than one.
The argument is also only defined up to adding $2\pi k$; the value in $(-\pi, \pi]$ is the
**principal argument**.

## Why bother

Because **multiplication becomes trivial**. Multiply the moduli, add the arguments:

$$
z_1z_2 = r_1r_2\left[\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) + i\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\right]
$$

$$
\frac{z_1}{z_2} = \frac{r_1}{r_2}\left[\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2) + i\sin(\theta_1-\theta_2)\right]
$$

(It falls out of expanding the product and applying the angle-addition identities from
[[Trigonometric Function]].) Compare with the rectangular version in [[Complex Numbers]], which
needs four multiplications and a sign rule.

More importantly, it says what complex multiplication **is**: *multiplying by $z$ scales by $|z|$
and rotates by $\arg z$*. Multiplying by $i$ ($r=1$, $\theta = \pi/2$) is rotation by $90°$, and
$i^2 = -1$ becomes the observation that two $90°$ turns face you backwards. Rectangular form
hides this completely.

## De Moivre's Theorem

$$
\left[r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\right]^n = r^n\left(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta\right)
$$

Just the multiplication rule applied $n$ times, and it makes powers a one-line computation.
$(1+i)^{10}$ is unpleasant by binomial expansion; in polar form $1+i$ has $r=\sqrt{2}$ and
$\theta = \pi/4$, so the answer is $2^5(\cos\frac{10\pi}{4} + i\sin\frac{10\pi}{4}) = 32i$.

It works for fractional $n$ too, which gives the **$n$th roots**: $z$ has exactly $n$ distinct
$n$th roots,

$$
z^{1/n} = r^{1/n}\left[\cos\frac{\theta + 2\pi k}{n} + i\sin\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}\right],
\qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1
$$

They sit evenly spaced on a circle of radius $r^{1/n}$, $2\pi/n$ apart. The $n$th roots of unity
are the $n$ corners of a regular $n$-gon on the unit circle starting at $1$. **That picture is
what the fast Fourier transform is built on**, since the FFT's divide-and-conquer step exploits
the symmetry of those roots. See [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]].

## Euler's formula

$$
e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
z = re^{i\theta}
$$

The exponential form, and it is where this material is genuinely heading. It makes every rule
above a property of exponents you already know: $e^{i\theta_1}e^{i\theta_2} =
e^{i(\theta_1+\theta_2)}$ **is** the add-the-arguments rule, and De Moivre is just
$(e^{i\theta})^n = e^{in\theta}$.

Setting $\theta = \pi$ gives $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$. Rearranged, it gives $\cos$ and $\sin$ in terms
of exponentials, which is why [[Fourier Series]] can be written far more compactly in complex
form than as separate sine and cosine sums. Taken properly in
[[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]]; this course sets it up.

## Related

- [[Complex Numbers]] for arithmetic and conjugates
- [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]]: complex eigenvalues have a modulus (growth per step) and an
  argument (rotation per step), which is exactly the polar reading
- [[Linear Transformation]]: the rotation matrix is multiplication by $e^{i\theta}$ written in
  $\mathbb{R}^2$
- [[Trigonometric Function]] in [[CALCULUS 1]] for the identities underneath
- [[Polar Coordinates]] in [[CALCULUS 2]] is the same conversion applied to a **point in the
  plane** rather than to a complex number: identical formulas, different object. That note owns
  graphing $r = f(\theta)$, polar area, and arc length; this one owns modulus, argument, De Moivre,
  and Euler. Neither restates the other
- [[Roots of Unity]] in [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] is De Moivre's theorem cashed out: the
  $n$ solutions of $z^n = 1$ are the angles that reach a multiple of $2\pi$ when multiplied by $n$.
  They are the entries of the [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] matrix, so this note is where the
  whole discrete transform comes from
